CausalChain: Chronic ethanol exposure -> Impairment of hepatocellular autophagy -> p62 accumulation -> Sequestration of Keap1 -> Sustained Nrf2 activation -> (a) Initial antioxidant protection and (b) Shift to anabolic reprogramming (lipogenesis and proliferation) -> Amplification by concurrent retinoid signaling disruption -> Increased risk of progression from ALD to HCC
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that chronic alcohol exposure disrupts hepatocyte autophagy, leading to the accumulation of p62. The build-up of p62 sequesters Keap1, thereby resulting in sustained Nrf2 activation. Initially, Nrf2 activation confers protection by mitigating oxidative stress; however, when persistent it drives a metabolic shift characterized by increased lipogenesis and cellular proliferation. This anabolic reprogramming is further exacerbated by ethanol-induced impairment of retinoid signaling and potential interactions with inflammatory pathways, collectively promoting the transition from alcoholic liver disease to hepatocellular carcinoma. The hypothesis will be examined via advanced CRISPR screening and single-cell transcriptomic analyses to map the dynamic changes in Nrf2 activity and metabolic gene expression over time, thereby determining the precise conditions under which Nrf2’s role shifts from cytoprotection to oncogenesis.
Abstract: Chronic alcohol exposure is known to disrupt cellular homeostasis in the liver, yet the sequential molecular events driving the progression from alcoholic liver disease (ALD) to hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remain incompletely understood. We propose that ethanol-dependent impairment of hepatocellular autophagy results in the accumulation of p62, which sequesters Keap1, leading to sustained activation of the transcription factor Nrf2. Initially, this Nrf2 activation mitigates oxidative stress; however, when persistent it induces an anabolic reprogramming that promotes lipogenesis and cellular proliferation. Moreover, our revised hypothesis integrates evidence of alcohol-induced disruption of retinoid signaling and other modulators of cell fate, suggesting that these parallel pathways further amplify Nrf2’s switch from a cytoprotective to an oncogenic driver. This model will be rigorously tested using contemporary approaches including CRISPR-based gene editing, high-resolution live-cell imaging, and single-cell multi-omics to delineate the temporal thresholds and dose-dependent transitions in Nrf2 activity that underlie this progression.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis centered on chronic alcohol exposure impairing autophagy, leading to p62 accumulation, Keap1 sequestration, and sustained Nrf2 activation, which shifts from protecting against oxidative stress to promoting lipogenesis and proliferation culminating in HCC. The revised hypothesis retains these core steps but explicitly integrates recent observational evidence and acknowledges alternative signaling pathways—particularly the disruption of retinoid signaling—that may interact with the p62/Keap1/Nrf2 axis. Additionally, the new version enhances practical implementability by proposing the use of advanced technologies (e.g., CRISPR-based gene editing, live-cell imaging, and single-cell multi-omics) to precisely delineate the temporal and quantitative thresholds of Nrf2’s dual role, thereby addressing previously identified gaps regarding mechanistic detail and context specificity.
